summary: A 1971 note by R. B. Kalin on implementation of interrupt keys, about letting a user interrupt a remote program.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 103 proposes placing a special character in the input stream where an interrupt occurs. The remote system also receives an INS control message, suspends the process and scans for the marker to find where input should switch.

subtitle: A proposed marker to synchronize a remote interrupt with keyboard input.

tldr.problem: The NCP can suspend a remote process, but control messages on a separate link do not show where the keyboard input stream should switch to a supervisory process.
tldr.mechanism: For ASCII data streams, the proposal inserts an interrupt sync character, octal 200, at the interrupt point and pairs it with an INS control message.
tldr.outcome: The author presents this as a specific patch, notes its limitations and says a comprehensive solution would require larger NCP changes.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 103 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC presents a specific interrupt-synchronization patch and says a comprehensive solution would need a major NCP revision.

sections.title: Why Interrupts Need a Stream Marker
sections.content:
An interrupt key suspends the current user process and switches later keyboard input to a supervisory process. Input typed before the interrupt may remain buffered for the suspended process.

The current NCP can suspend a remote process with INS and INR control messages, but those messages travel on a separate link from keyboard input. Their arrival times therefore do not tell the receiving host which characters belong to each process.
sections.plainLanguage: The remote system needs to know exactly where typing changes from the user process to the supervisor. A control message on another link does not identify that position in the input stream.

sections.title: Interrupt Sync Character and INS
sections.content:
For ASCII data streams, the proposal uses eight-bit fields for characters and puts an interrupt sync character with code octal 200 in the data stream at the point of interruption. Codes from octal 201 to octal 377 are to be ignored by a receiving host and reserved for possible control information.

The sender also sends an INS control message when it inserts the sync character. The foreign host immediately suspends the attached process and scans the input stream. Once it finds the marker, it switches the stream to the supervisory process; input before the marker should be buffered for the suspended process if possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The marker travels with the typed data, so it shows where the interrupt happened. INS tells the remote host to suspend the process and look for that marker.

sections.title: Ordering the Marker and Control Message
sections.content:
The INS message is retained because there may not be enough allocation to send the text message containing the sync character. If the sync character arrives before the matching INS, the user process should be suspended and the NCP should wait for INS before proceeding.

If the host cannot buffer all input for the user process, the proposal allows it to discard that input and return an error message through the supervisory process. It requires outstanding input to be consumed and message buffers freed so pending character messages can be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The separate INS message backs up the marker if the data cannot be sent yet. The receiver waits for both pieces and must free buffers so pending input can move.

sections.title: Limits of the Proposed Patch
sections.content:
The author says the method works only for seven-bit character streams and does not cover EBCDIC, ASCII-8 or other larger character sets. It requires the receiving system to scan data on interruptable connections.

The method cannot handle lost character boundaries or unmatched INS messages and sync characters. If either message fails to reach the remote host, the remote process may loop indefinitely. The RFC says a comprehensive solution would require more than minor changes to the current NCP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal has limits: it supports only seven-bit character streams and depends on both marker and control messages arriving in order. If one is lost, the remote process may not recover.
